title: Quarterly Ready
user: UK sole traders, tutors, and landlords who need to keep compliant digital records and submit Making Tax Digital quarterly updates without learning a full accounting suite.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The asker says April 2026 MTD starts above £50k and that freelancers and tutors using spreadsheets often did not know; commenters call Xero/Excel too hard and say they would use a focused tool.

A separate builder describes UK MTD bookkeeping as compliance-heavy, including bank import, receipt matching, merchant rules, and an accountant share link; a commenter objects to being forced into a third party.
Invoice Ninja users report that a fixed late fee is not compliant with European law and need calculation and explanatory wording that reflects local rules.

recurrence: Two independent 2026 UK discussions describe the deadline, spreadsheet dependence, and accountant handoff; regulatory mistakes and missed submissions make the pain high-severity and recurring quarterly.
current_workaround: Spreadsheets or notes, then a bookkeeper; some buy Xero-like suites they find too broad, or build their own software.
incumbents_and_gap: Xero, QuickBooks, FreeAgent, and Sage cover full accounting but impose a general ledger-first experience. The gap is a guided MTD record-to-quarterly-update workflow with clear review and accountant handoff, not another generic ledger.
smallest_useful_product: UK-only web app: transaction/receipt capture, category review, quarter checklist, accountant read-only pack, and HMRC-compatible submission via an approved integration. Non-goals: payroll, international tax, lending, or autonomous tax advice.
success_measure: In a 2026 pilot, 70% of activated users reconcile their first quarter and export/share a complete accountant pack before its deadline; fewer than 5% need manual support to find an unresolved transaction.
monetization: subscription — £12/month or £99/year is justified by a recurring statutory deadline and ongoing record retention.
constraints: HMRC MTD recognition/integration requirements, UK GDPR, financial-data encryption, audit trails, conservative tax copy, and explicit human review before submission.
why_distinct: It is a compliance runway and handoff product for one imminent regime, not a replacement accounting system or an LLM tax adviser.

title: Close Pack
user: Owners of small multi-entity SaaS and service businesses who need to give a CPA a defensible, complete month-end package without replacing their accounting system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A multi-business owner is leaving rising-price QuickBooks but says their CPA and tax team still need access; the thread highlights accountant compatibility and auditability as the migration blocker.
A SaaS owner asks for bookkeeping/accounting help, is unhappy with the service around QuickBooks, and needs sales-tax expertise across states.
The request explicitly asks for a tax-support package that joins transactions with receipts, invoices, reimbursements, and evidence, since notes and exports alone do not answer audit questions.

recurrence: Separate owners in 2025–26 report the same dependency: accountants need usable records, while the business owner needs control, tax support, and less vendor lock-in. Close work repeats monthly and at year end.
current_workaround: Grant broad QuickBooks access, export CSVs, email receipts, and answer repeated CPA follow-ups from several drives and inboxes.
incumbents_and_gap: QuickBooks and Xero are systems of record; Dext and Hubdoc collect documents. None makes a vendor-neutral, CPA-readable close packet with evidence completeness and unanswered-question tracking the core deliverable.
smallest_useful_product: Read-only connectors/imports for bank CSV, QuickBooks/Xero exports, and document folders; produce a period close checklist, transaction-to-evidence index, accountant comments, and immutable export. Non-goals: posting journal entries, filing tax returns, or bookkeeping automation.
success_measure: Pilot accountants close a monthly client file with 30% fewer evidence requests, measured against the prior three closes.
monetization: subscription — $39/month per business (with accountant seats) aligns to a repeated close workflow and avoids replacing the ledger.
constraints: Financial/PII encryption, least-privilege OAuth, retention controls, audit logs, tax-record retention disclosures, and no claim that the pack constitutes accounting advice.
why_distinct: It improves the handoff boundary between owner and accountant instead of becoming yet another bookkeeping ledger.

title: Client Action Room
user: Small agencies and professional-service firms that need clients to complete a few time-sensitive requests—approve, upload, choose, or pay—without exposing a full project-management system.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo developer says HoneyBook was expensive and fragmented tools forced them to build a white-label portal for file sharing, project tracking, and invoices; a commenter notes firms want zero operational overhead.
A five-year freelancer reports multi-client work became messy across tasks, documents, knowledge, and several client platforms; clients liked having one secure portal.
This 27-reaction Odoo request says client portal blocks are hard-coded; repeatedly building custom modules just to hide, filter, rename, or tailor client data is costly and frustrating.

recurrence: Two independent agency/freelancer implementations and a high-interest ERP request show the portal is repeatedly rebuilt because the essential client-facing actions are too rigid or bundled with large suites.
current_workaround: Email links, Drive/Notion folders, Slack, invoices, and project trackers; some self-host a portal or buy HoneyBook/Worksuite-class platforms.
incumbents_and_gap: HoneyBook, Clientjoy, Odoo, and project-management tools provide broad portals. Their gap is a fast, configurable action inbox for an external client, with no client account required for low-risk tasks.
smallest_useful_product: Branded portal links with a deadline-based action queue, secure uploads, approval forms, payment/booking links, reminders, and a staff audit trail. Non-goals: task boards, CRM replacement, document editing, or general chat.
success_measure: In pilots, 60% of requested client actions complete within 72 hours and agencies reduce follow-up emails per action by at least 40%.
monetization: subscription — $49/month for five client workspaces, because firms repeatedly chase actions and need branded, retained records.
constraints: Role-scoped links, expiring uploads, malware scanning, audit records, data-residency controls, and clear e-signature limitations unless regulated signing is added later.
why_distinct: The primary object is an accountable external action, not a generic portal, CRM, or project board.

title: Worklog Bridge
user: Freelance developers and small software consultancies who must turn Git/calendar activity into client-reviewable billable work without surveillance software.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelance developer built a Git-history tool because reconstructing client work from calendars and commits at month-end took too much time; it creates a shareable approval timesheet.
A separate time-tracking launch reports users generating timesheets from screen context, while a commenter wants local processing rather than trusting a third party with screen recording.
Kimai users request direct two-way Outlook calendar integration for exporting and syncing timesheet entries, showing that manual reconstruction remains unresolved.

recurrence: Three 2025–26 signals cover Git, calendar, and screenshot-derived reconstruction; month-end billing turns it into a recurring revenue-risk problem, with a privacy constraint.
current_workaround: Search commits and calendar events manually, fill a timesheet, run intrusive screenshot trackers, or maintain separate tools that do not reconcile.
incumbents_and_gap: Toggl, Harvest, Clockify, Kimai, and Hubstaff track time, but they expect proactive timers or surveillance. The gap is privacy-preserving evidence reconstruction plus a concise client approval artifact.
smallest_useful_product: Local desktop collector reads opt-in Git metadata and selected calendar events, lets the worker confirm/redact weekly narratives, and publishes a client approval link with immutable acceptance. Non-goals: screenshots, keystroke monitoring, payroll, or automated invoicing.
success_measure: At least 75% of pilot users generate a weekly draft in under five minutes and have 90% of billable entries approved without a clarification round.
monetization: subscription — $12/user/month funds calendar integrations and durable approval records while remaining far below agency time-suite pricing.
constraints: Local-first processing, explicit source selection, redaction before sharing, no content capture by default, OAuth minimization, and immutable but privacy-preserving approval receipts.
why_distinct: It reconstructs and verifies professional work without turning workers into monitored activity streams.

title: Reminder Proof
user: Independent dental and outpatient clinics that need reliable appointment reminders, delivery proof, and fallbacks without replacing their EMR.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A dental-clinic software builder spent weeks on WhatsApp appointment reminders, was rejected repeatedly in verification, then had the account banned after three template messages without a useful appeal path.
OpenEMR’s reminder runner can fail when no reminders are due and has recurring-event and status-update problems, showing that reminder delivery must be observable rather than assumed.
A customer could select an apparently free appointment slot but received a no-available-users error, demonstrating the operational cost of opaque calendar synchronization failures.

recurrence: Three separate scheduling/reminder failure modes in 2025–26—provider account loss, reminder runner faults, and calendar mismatch—can directly create no-shows and staff callbacks.
current_workaround: Staff manually text/call patients, rely on one channel such as WhatsApp, or troubleshoot inside an EMR/calendar after a complaint.
incumbents_and_gap: OpenEMR, Cal.com, NexHealth, and reminder vendors own scheduling or messaging. Smaller clinics lack a vendor-neutral delivery ledger that retries across approved channels and makes failures actionable to front desk staff.
smallest_useful_product: EMR/calendar connector, consent-aware template sender, SMS/email/approved WhatsApp fallback policy, delivery/response timeline, and staff exception queue. Non-goals: clinical notes, diagnosis, full scheduling, or unapproved bulk messaging.
success_measure: A clinic records delivery or a staff-owned exception for 99% of scheduled reminder attempts and reduces reminder-related no-shows by 15% within 90 days.
monetization: subscription — $79/location/month plus messaging pass-through fits a recurring appointment volume and measurable no-show cost.
constraints: HIPAA/UK GDPR as applicable, patient consent/opt-out, minimal PHI, BAA/DPA readiness, jurisdictional SMS rules, and no medical advice.
why_distinct: It is a reliability and proof layer around an existing calendar/EMR, not another clinical management suite.

title: Parts Promise
user: Solo-to-20-person electricians, HVAC, and repair firms that must promise a job date only when the required part is truly allocated to that job.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A solo carpenter says Jobber cost $150+/month and was bloated for the three needs they actually had: invoicing, scheduling, and client management.

An Ask HN thread specifically asks what has worked when deploying tools in trade or field-service businesses; a responder describes electrical-job workflows across job finding and qualified worker coordination.
The request says aggregate 'on order' quantities do not show whether a specific build/job is covered, forcing manual notes, PO checks, memory, and risking duplicate orders.

recurrence: Tradespeople report price/bloat pressure while a production-inventory user details the same allocation ambiguity that causes repeat purchases and broken customer promises. It arises on every parts-dependent job.
current_workaround: Keep job schedules in field-service software, call suppliers, track parts in spreadsheets or notes, and infer whether generic stock/on-order totals cover the job.
incumbents_and_gap: Jobber, Tradify, ServiceTitan, and ERPs cover broad field service or inventory. The wedge is job-level parts commitment and supplier ETA evidence without buying an enterprise dispatch/ERP stack.
smallest_useful_product: Mobile job card with required-part list, scan/manual allocation from van/warehouse/supplier PO, ETA confidence, customer-date warning, and reorder suggestion. Non-goals: payroll, dispatch optimization, full inventory accounting, or marketplace lead generation.
success_measure: Pilot firms reduce duplicate part orders by 25% and log an attributable parts status for 90% of jobs that require a non-stock item.
monetization: subscription — $39/month base plus $8/technician is tied to daily field use and avoided repeat materials/visits.
constraints: Offline conflict handling, barcode/device permissions, supplier-data licensing, no inaccurate availability guarantees, and regional tax/unit support.
why_distinct: It protects a customer promise through part-to-job attribution rather than cloning a full field-service suite.

title: Receipt Recovery
user: Freelancers and small-business owners who need to capture a receipt in the moment and later prove which bank transaction it supports, even when mobile connectivity is unreliable.

evidence.quote_or_summary: The builder calls manual receipt-to-bank-transaction reconciliation a major bookkeeping pain; commenters ask for integrations and describe matching/categorizing transactions as an almost daily chore.
Expensify documents that backgrounding a mobile app during receipt scanning can leave a stuck expense, a failed upload, or even removal of the uploaded receipt.

recurrence: Receipt matching is described as daily work, while the mobile failure report shows evidence can be lost precisely when capture happens in the field; the need recurs for every deductible purchase.
current_workaround: Photograph receipts into a camera roll, email them to oneself, re-scan in expense software, or reconcile manually at month end.
incumbents_and_gap: Expensify, Dext, Hubdoc, QuickBooks, and Xero provide receipt features, but smaller operators still need capture confirmation, a recoverable local queue, and an evidence-to-transaction queue without adopting a full expense program.
smallest_useful_product: Offline-first mobile receipt vault with durable local upload queue, capture receipt hash/date, optional bank CSV/OFX import, human-confirmed matching, and exportable tax folder. Non-goals: OCR-led auto-bookkeeping, card issuance, reimbursement approvals, or financial advice.
success_measure: In pilot use, 99.5% of captured receipts reach the vault after connectivity returns and 70% of imported transactions are matched or explicitly marked unsupported within seven days.
monetization: subscription — $8/month is supportable for ongoing storage, bank imports, and tax-season retrieval, with a free capped capture tier.
constraints: Encrypted device/server storage, backup/export clarity, receipt retention requirements, bank-import security, and no claim that OCR classifications are authoritative.
why_distinct: The wedge is guaranteed evidence recovery and explicit match confidence, not an AI receipt scanner or a corporate-expense clone.

title: Intake Desk
user: 10–100-person distributors, workshops, and small manufacturers that receive supplier deliveries against purchase orders but are not ready to implement an ERP.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A team describes smaller companies running procurement in spreadsheets/email: missed orders, lost documents, manual packing-list matching, and slow goods receipt; they say ERP alternatives were too heavy and expensive.
A current ERP issue reports that goods reception cannot load the items from a supplier order and can create only an empty reception—the precise intake step that must be dependable.

recurrence: The 2026 SMB procurement report describes repeated order, document, and warehouse intake chaos; a separate ERP issue confirms receiving is a brittle critical path rather than a solved spreadsheet replacement.
current_workaround: Email POs, print packing lists, check quantities by hand, update spreadsheets, then chase suppliers for status.
incumbents_and_gap: Odoo, Dolibarr, NetSuite, Cin7, and procure-to-pay suites are broad and setup-heavy. The gap is a one-day receiving desk that can start from CSV/email POs and create a trustworthy discrepancy record.
smallest_useful_product: Supplier PO inbox, QR/phone receiving, expected-versus-received scan/count, photo/doc attachment, discrepancy/partial-delivery workflow, and accounting/ERP CSV export. Non-goals: general ledger, warehouse management system, forecasting, or supplier marketplace.
success_measure: A pilot warehouse records 95% of deliveries on the day received and cuts time from arrival to discrepancy notification by 50%.
monetization: subscription — $149/site/month supports a workflow used by receiving staff every day and is materially cheaper than an ERP project.
constraints: Offline-capable scanning, hardware/browser compatibility, document retention, accurate unit conversion, immutable receipt audit trail, and integration import validation.
why_distinct: It starts at the receiving dock and produces evidence of exceptions, instead of competing as a full procurement or ERP platform.

title: Batch Proofbook
user: Small-batch food, cosmetics, candle, and craft manufacturers that must retain lot, ingredient, label, and production evidence without enterprise manufacturing software.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A micro-bakery software search found existing tools expensive and generic despite straightforward small-batch workflows; the resulting product includes lot traceability, expiry, allergen flags, recipes, and receiving.
A scheduled document-retention workflow ran years early on 2,273 documents, illustrating that retention/expiry automation needs a reviewable record rather than silent background behavior.

recurrence: The small-manufacturer case spans recipes, lots, expiry, labels, and purchase receipts; evidence retention recurs for every batch and becomes high-severity in a recall, inspection, or customer complaint.
current_workaround: Spreadsheets, paper batch sheets, Drive folders, generic inventory/recipe apps, and memory; retention dates are handled with calendar reminders or brittle automation.
incumbents_and_gap: Craftybase, Katana, MRPeasy, Odoo, and full QMS tools are either broad, priced for larger manufacturers, or do not make a compact recall-ready evidence bundle the center of use.
smallest_useful_product: Batch record from ingredient receipt to finished lot: recipe version, supplier/lot link, photos/labels, manual checkoffs, expiry/hold timer, and one-click recall/export bundle. Non-goals: e-commerce, MRP optimization, HACCP consulting, or regulatory certification claims.
success_measure: Pilot makers can assemble a complete traceability pack for a chosen finished lot in under 10 minutes, and 90% of new batches include all required checkoffs.
monetization: subscription — $49/month/site is aligned with ongoing batch records and is viable below industrial MRP/QMS pricing.
constraints: Jurisdiction-specific food/cosmetic rules, offline device sync, immutable revisions, retention safeguards, data export, and clear disclaimer that the product does not certify compliance.
why_distinct: It is a lightweight proof-of-batch system, not generic inventory, recipe management, or an enterprise QMS.

title: Service Proof Loop
user: Recurring cleaning and maintenance businesses that need post-job proof, client feedback, and approved extras to flow into the next visit without building a custom customer portal.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A freelancer says post-project feedback is often forgotten or arrives as vague email/DM replies, and built a no-login feedback form to make it easier for clients to respond.
A service-business client-portal request calls for job history, evidence photos, automatic post-job ratings, and extras requests attached to the next scheduled job card.

recurrence: A feedback collection pain and a detailed 2026 service portal specification converge on the same loop: crews finish work, clients need proof and a low-friction way to request/approve the next action.
current_workaround: Text photos, ask for reviews manually, retain notes in a CRM, and retype client requests into the next job card.
incumbents_and_gap: Jobber, Housecall Pro, Worksuite, and customer-survey products cover parts of the loop. The gap is an after-visit proof-to-next-visit workflow that works over a secure link, without a customer app or broad CRM migration.
smallest_useful_product: Technician upload/checklist, client proof page, one-tap accept/problem/rating, configurable extras, and automatic attachment to the next recurring job export. Non-goals: dispatch, payments, payroll, public-review solicitation campaigns, or worker tracking.
success_measure: At least 40% of completed recurring jobs receive a client response within 48 hours and 80% of requested extras arrive on the next job card without staff re-entry.
monetization: subscription — $59/month per business plus technician seats follows recurring-job volume and saves office re-entry work.
constraints: Consent for photos/messages, tenant isolation, abuse/reporting controls, secure expiring share links, regional consumer-review rules, and no storage of unnecessary home-entry details.
why_distinct: The product closes the operational loop from completed visit to an actionable next visit, not just feedback collection or a generic client portal.

title: Integration Handoff Room
user: Small software agencies and fractional engineering teams that need clients to accept an API integration with executable examples, decisions, and ownership—not a pile of docs and email.

evidence.quote_or_summary: A small dev team has onboarding, design, API, and operational docs scattered across Notion, Drive, GitHub, and Slack and wants something that stays easy to maintain and sync.
The request explains that API developers and QA need reusable valid/invalid/localized request variants for debugging, regression, and team handoff; it asks for persisted multi-payload request tabs.

recurrence: The two 2025 threads identify the same delivery gap: documentation is scattered while the actual payloads needed to verify the integration live in personal tooling. This recurs at every client release and handoff.
current_workaround: Send Notion/Drive links, share Postman/Bruno collections, run screen-share acceptance calls, and reconstruct what was agreed when support begins.
incumbents_and_gap: Notion, Confluence, Postman, Bruno, and Stoplight manage docs or requests. None is a small agency-facing acceptance room that binds a selected executable example, a decision, and a named client acknowledgement.
smallest_useful_product: Git-connected release room that embeds sanitized request/response fixtures, acceptance checklist, client questions, versioned decisions, and signed-off handover export. Non-goals: API gateway, test runner, source-code hosting, or general wiki.
success_measure: In pilot projects, 80% of client integration questions are answered from the handoff room and post-handoff clarification hours decline by 30%.
monetization: subscription — $79/month per agency for active client rooms, because the value repeats with every delivery while the client gets free reviewer access.
constraints: Never store live secrets, automatic fixture redaction, repository OAuth least privilege, export/delete controls, and legal clarity that acknowledgement is not a substitute for a contract.
why_distinct: It turns handoff into a verified client-facing artifact rather than trying to replace a docs platform or API client.

title: Commitment Radar
user: Freelancers and tiny teams that need a private, complete view of recurring software and supplier commitments before an unexpected renewal, cancellation deadline, or budget review.

evidence.quote_or_summary: An Ask HN user proposes an end-to-end-encrypted expense browser extension specifically to log Stripe Checkout activity and active subscriptions across devices, asking whether people would want it.
Expensify’s requested receipt review redesign needs the full receipt image and expense details visible together, reinforcing that raw transactions alone are insufficient for financial review.

recurrence: A direct subscription-tracking request plus a large expense-review workflow point to recurring spend records that need the original merchant terms/receipt; the event repeats with each renewal and card charge.
current_workaround: Search email, scan bank statements, keep a spreadsheet, or discover subscriptions after a charge; supporting receipts remain in inboxes or expense tools.
incumbents_and_gap: Rocket Money, Ramp, Brex, QuickBooks, and expense suites either target consumers/large businesses, require bank/card control, or do not preserve the purchase evidence and cancellation terms for a tiny team’s operational commitments.
smallest_useful_product: Privacy-first browser extension plus web vault: capture checkout confirmation with user approval, extract merchant/renewal/cancellation date, attach receipt, calendar/email reminder, and owner/decision status. Non-goals: bank aggregation, card issuing, automated cancellation, or financial advice.
success_measure: Among activated teams, 70% assign an owner and renewal decision to every detected recurring commitment within 30 days; pilots report at least one avoided unwanted renewal per 20 accounts.
monetization: subscription — $10/month for solo users and $29/team funds encrypted sync and recurring monitoring without monetizing transaction data.
constraints: Explicit page-level capture consent, encrypted storage, browser-store policies, no credential scraping, data export/deletion, and conservative merchant/renewal extraction with user confirmation.
why_distinct: It manages the evidence and decision behind a commitment, not merely a list of subscriptions or a bank-feed budgeting dashboard.
